t: LeetCode 2241 - Design an ATM Machine: Greedy Denomination Dispensing
o: **Understanding the problem.** We maintain five counters, one per denomination (20, 50, 100, 200, 500), updated by `deposit` and consulted by `withdraw`. Withdrawal is a forced greedy sweep: from the largest note down to the smallest, hand out as many notes as possible (`min(count[i], amount // note[i])`). The greedy can strand an amount - withdrawing 600 with a lone $500 note leaves $100 that no smaller note can cover, so the request is rejected and the vault must stay untouched. That is why we stage the full dispensing plan first and commit it only when the remainder reaches zero. Deposits reach one billion per denomination, so counters need 64-bit storage in statically typed languages.
k: Largest-note-first greedy is mandated by the machine rules, not chosen for optimality - even when it fails, substitution is forbidden.
Validate before mutating state: compute every `take` count, then deduct only if the remaining amount is zero.
Counts and products like count times denomination reach the billion scale, requiring 64-bit arithmetic in Java/C++.

a.n: Approach 1: Denomination Counters with Staged Greedy Withdrawal
a.i: Store the five counters plus the fixed denomination values. On withdrawal, sweep from the biggest note to the smallest, tentatively taking as many notes as possible at each step; if any amount remains at the end the request fails and nothing changes, otherwise commit the tentative plan to the counters. Both operations touch only five slots, hence constant time per call.
s: `deposit`: add each incoming batch entry to the matching counter.
`withdraw`: for `i` from 4 down to 0, set `take[i] = min(count[i], amount // note[i])` and reduce the remaining amount by `take[i] * note[i]`.
If the remaining amount is positive, return `[-1]` without modifying state.
Otherwise subtract `take[i]` from every counter and return `take`.
a.t: O(1) per operation - both methods touch exactly five counters.
a.sp: O(1) - fixed-size state of five counters.

w: There is essentially one correct design here, so spend your interview time on the edge cases. The classic bug is mutating counters during the scan and corrupting vault state on a rejected withdrawal - always validate, then commit. Replaying the worked example helps: after depositing [0,0,1,2,1], withdraw(600) succeeds via 100+500, but a later withdraw(600) with [0,1,0,3,1] fails because greedy takes 500 first and cannot finish. A likely follow-up: support arbitrary denominations (keep them sorted descending), or decide whether ANY mix of notes could fulfill a request - a different feasibility question solvable with DP over the counters.
